vignette:
Marisol is a 27-year-old HVAC technician who came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to handle things on her own. She is one of the few women on her service team, and before the trauma she had taken pride in being steady under pressure, willing to go into hot attics, cramped utility rooms, and unfamiliar buildings without much hesitation. The event she describes happened when she was being held and tortured in a setting where she felt completely trapped, with no way out and no one coming to help. In telling it, she does not offer a smooth narrative. She reaches a point and goes quiet, her face tightening, and says that when the memory comes back it hits all at once, so intensely that she has to stop. What she does say makes clear why certain moments in ordinary life have become so charged. During the ordeal, she was confined with no options, unable to leave, and exposed to a female perpetrator whose presence became fused in her mind with danger and humiliation. She recalls seeing injuries up close—wounds on bodies, damaged skin, blood—and now even brief glimpses of visible injuries on other people can abruptly pull her back toward that same emotional state.

In the first weeks afterward, Marisol noticed that the memory did not feel like a normal memory. At times she would describe it as if it had happened to someone else, as though it belonged to another person and not to her. Yet when something brushed against it, the distance collapsed and she was flooded with shame so intense that she could barely stay with it. What was hardest to bear was not only fear but the feeling that something about her had been exposed, broken, or contaminated. She had come to believe that she had permanently changed for the worse. The self she had trusted before—practical, decisive, capable in tight spaces and difficult jobs—no longer felt dependable to her. She became uncertain of her own judgment and was often preoccupied with the thought that she could not trust herself to do the right thing when it mattered.

Those beliefs sat beside a broad sense that danger could come from anyone. She was certain now that you can never really know who will harm you. That conviction showed up in small, repetitive routines. At night she checked doors and windows multiple times before trying to sleep, even in her apartment where she lived alone. If she did fall asleep, she often woke suddenly and alert, getting out of bed to make sure she was safe and that the locks were still secured. Sudden noises made her jump. A bang in the building hallway, a tool dropped in the shop, a customer appearing unexpectedly behind her could send a jolt through her body before she could think.

Her work as an HVAC technician put her into exactly the kinds of situations she now found difficult to tolerate. Service calls often required entering private homes, walking through tight mechanical closets, basements, and locked utility areas, and being alone with customers. She became especially tense when a call meant being alone in a house with a woman. She did not tell coworkers why, but she started trying to swap those assignments, lingering by the dispatch board to see if someone else could take them. When that was not possible, she would keep doors open whenever she could, position herself near an exit, and feel panicky if she had no easy way out of a room. On one job, a female customer stood nearby while Marisol worked in a narrow laundry space, and Marisol became so overwhelmed by the sense of being cornered that she cut the visit short and later told her supervisor she was feeling sick. On another day, seeing a coworker’s badly scraped forearm during a repair caused her to abruptly look away and leave the area under the pretense of getting a tool.

Over time these patterns narrowed her life. She avoided being alone socially with women when she could do so without explanation, which left her more isolated and guarded. At work, her efforts to manage assignments and keep control over exits made her seem distant and inflexible, and she worried that others were noticing. What finally brought her in was a recent stretch of broken sleep and increasing strain on the job after she startled badly during a service call and then spent the night waking to check locks. She said she was tired of living like every space had to be assessed for escape and every person might be dangerous. At the same time, she was frightened that talking directly about what happened would prove that the damage is permanent, or that she would become so overwhelmed she would lose control completely. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase the past but to feel that her life belongs to her again.
